caseno: FA No. 66 of 2004 with FMA No. 94 of 2004 with FA No. 10 of 2005 and C. Rule 394(F) of 2004
lawyer:
AKM Abdul Hakim with Md Joynul Abedin, Advocates—For the Appellant in FA No. 66 of 2004 and FMA No. 94 of 2004 and for Respondent in FA No. 10 of 2005.
Rafiqul Islam Miah with Md Saifur Rahman, Advocates—For Respondent in FA No. 66 of 2004 and FMA No. 94 of 2004 and for Appellant in FA No. 10 of 2005
parties:
Bangladesh Water Development Board ------ Defendant-Appellant 
vs 
Titas Prokaushali Ltd. ------ Plaintiff Respondent
full_judgment:
2. These appeals are against the judgment and order dated 16-10-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka, in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 12 of 2003 refusing to set aside the award dated 14-9-2002 passed by the learned Umpire and making the same a rule of the Court. The Bangladesh Water Development Board as the appellants preferred appeal Nos. 66 of 2004 and 94 of 2004 whereas the Titas Prokaushali Ltd filed appeal No. 10 of 2005 for refusing to grant interest on the awarded sum. 

 3. After filing of the award in the aforesaid Court the appellant of Appeal No. 66 of 2004 filed an objection under section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 (hereinafter called 'the Act') and the self-same appellate also filed an application under section 33 read with section 30 of the Act for setting aside the award which was registered as Miscellaneous Arbitration Case No. 64 of 2000. Both the aforesaid Title Suit along with the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case was heard by the trial Court analogously and by the impugned judgment the trial Court rejected the application filed by the appellant under section 33 of the Act and also rejected the objection filed by them under section 17 of the Act and made the award Rule of the Court by its order dated 16-10-2003. While making the award Rule of the Court the trial Court, however, modified the award by deleting the interest awarded by the Arbitrator/Umpire in favour of Titas Prokoushali Ltd (hereinafter called 'the contractor') and the contractor being aggrieved by that part of the impugned order preferred Appeal No. 10 of 2005 challenging that portion of the impugned decree of the trial Court. 

 5. This case has a chequered history. Initially, one Mr Abdul Barik Bhuiyan, Member, Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), was appointed as arbitrator on behalf of the owner and Advocate Mr Abdul Quddus, was appointed as an Arbitrator by the contractor but they, within the span of 3(three) years, could neither complete the arbitration proceeding nor took any step to get the time extended. As a result of which through the intervention of the Court the said arbitrators were removed and the present Arbitrators, namely, Mr Serajul Islam, a retired Additional Chief Engineer of BWDB was appointed Arbitrator on behalf of the owner and Mr Luthfe Alam, Advocate, was appointed Arbitrator by the contractor. On their appointment as Arbitrators they entered into the reference made by the parties and the contractor submitted their statement of claim where against the owner submitted a rejoinder denying the claim of the contractor. The contractor also submitted reply to the rejoinder of the owner. During the course of hearing before the Arbitrators both the parties produced the relevant papers before the Arbitrators and in the instant case salient feature of the case is that none of the documents produced by the parties have either been disputed by either of the parties and most of the documents are common documents. After the conclusion of the hearing and consideration of the materials by the learned Arbitrators they failed to agree with each other in respect of the claims made by the contractor. Mr Luthfe Alam, the learned Advocate, gave an award in favour of the contractor in respect of all the claims whereas Mr Serajul Islam rejected all the claims of the contractor except one, i.e., item No. 6, wherein he has given an award for Taka 28,800 with interest @ 6% out of claim of Taka 1,86,779. Therefore; essentially the matter was referred to an Umpire who was unanimously selected by the arbitrators, i.e., Mr Justice A. Jalil was appointed as umpire to finally resolve the dispute between the parties. The umpire on assumption of office notified the parties and after hearing them and considering the materials on record, in fact, concurred with the award given by Mr Luthfe Alam in respect of all the claims. However, in respect of two claims he has reduced the amount on ground of clerical mistake committed by Mr Alam but substantially maintained the award given by Mr Luthfe Alam. From the award of the Arbitrators as well as the award of the Umpire it appears that both the parties extensively argued their cases and placed all the relevant documents as they thought fit and proper. The learned Umpire out of total claim of Taka 3,29.28,569 gave the award on 14-9-2002 for Taka 1,70,37,641 along with interest @ 10% per annum till realisation and the said award after filing of it before the learned Additional Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka, was ultimately made a Rule of the Court and a decree was drawn on 16-10-2003 for Taka, 1,70,37,646, however, without any interest as the learned trial Court thought it fit not to award any interest on the principal sum given by the Umpire as the contractor is not a banking company. 

 6. We have perused the written objection filed by the appellant of Appeal No. 66 of 2004 as well as the application filed by them under section 33 read with section 30 of the Act. On a perusal of the same it appears that they have extensively argued their cases before the trial Court from their respective point of view. The owner assailed the award while the contractor supported the same and the learned trial Court after hearing the parties and considering the objection as well as the application filed under section 33 of the Act rejected both of them and made the award a Rule of the Court which gave rise to the present appeals: Here it may further be mentioned that in refusing to give interest on the awarded sum the learned trial Court observed that since the contractor is not a banking company it is not entitled to get any interest on the sum awarded and being aggrieved by that finding of the trial Court the contractor came up with the cross-appeal namely, First Appeal No. 10 of 2005. 

 8. The appeals were heard on several dates and all the materials that found place in the paper book, were placed before us by Mr Md Joynul Abedin but Mr Hakim as Senior Counsel for the appellant in the aforesaid two appeals came up with a straightforward and short submission. His most substantial submission was that in the instant case the learned trial Court in making the award a Rule of the Court and the learned Umpire making the award committed gross illegality and traveled beyond their jurisdiction in that the admitted position in law is that the agreement is the foundation of any arbitration proceeding and once a matter is referred to Arbitrators they are entitled to arbitrate only in respect of the matters referred to them as covered by the terms of the contract. In the instant case the Umpire in making the award lost sight of the fact that in the contract there is no provision for giving any compensation to the contractor in any event and it has been specifically provided for in the contract through Article 4.01 that the owner shall furnish the land upon which the work is to be done. If the contractor sustains a loss of time for delay in furnishing the lands or easement he is entitled to get extension of the contract time therefor. Therefore, it is specifically stated in the contract that if for some reason or other the owner is unable to hand over the land to the contractor within the specified time they are only entitled to get an extension of time and in the instant case the contractor was given that extension. Therefore, on this court they are not entitled to get any compensation for non-availability of the land as claimed by the contractor before the Arbitrators. This material aspect has been overlooked by the learned Arbitrator Mr Luthfe Alam as well as by the Umpire and therefore, in passing the award they have traveled beyond the terms of the contract which they are not authorised in law to do and this part of the award of the Umpire is beyond the terms of the contract and therefore by making the award he has committed jurisdictional error which in law amounts to judicial misconduct which is a valid ground for setting at naught any award passed by Arbitrator/Umpire. He then submits that this material and pertinent aspect of the case was also overlooked and/or missed by the learned trial Court and failing to appreciate the scope of arbitration and the authority of the Arbitrator the learned trial Court on misconception of law made the award Rule of the Court which ought to have been rejected by the Court in view of the aforesaid terms of the contract. The learned Advocate further elaborates his submission by drawing our attention to the contents of the contract documents and submits that it was known to the contractor before he participated in the bid that this protect would be carried out through the financial aid of Saudi Development Fund and a portion of that grant will be applied for this project and that is the only source of fund to meet the expenses of the project and that is why stringent terms were incorporated in the contract both in terms of time specification and quality of work. Within the four comers of the contract there is no stipulation which provides for any sort of compensation in the contract in the event of any breach if there be committed by the owner and knowing that well the contractor ventured to participate in the bid and ultimately entered into the contract with the owner. Therefore, he is also estopped by the principle of estoppel in raising any claim on that ground as well. The jurisdictional error committed by the Arbitrator/Umpire cuts at the root of the case and makes the award a nullity which is well established in law and to fortify his submission he has relied on the decision reported in (1991) 4 SCC 93, 57 DLR 626, (1999) 8 SCC 122 and AIR 2003(SC) 262, wherein it has been succinctly laid down by our Court as well as the Indian Supreme Court that if there be any jurisdictional error committed by the Arbitrator/ Umpire that nullifies the award, if any, given by the Arbitrator/Umpire. Mr Hakim then diverted his attention to Appeal No. 10 of 2005 which is on interest. By drawing our attention to the provision of section 29 of the Act he submitted that it is only the Court which is invested with the, discretion to give interest on the awarded amount but the Arbitrator has no authority whatsoever to give interest on the awarded amount and the law on this point has been well settled by our Appellate Division in the cases reported in 44 DLR (AD) 296 and 46 DLR (AD) 97. Drawing our attention 'particularly to the 46 DLR's case, Mr Hakim submitted that though the appellant of Appeal No. 10 of 2005 has heavily relied on that decision but, in fact, that decision does not come in aid of the appellant of Appeal No. 10 of 2005, inasmuch as in that case the trial Court refused to pass any order for interest. However, on appeal the High Court Division on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case took a view that there should be an order of interest and they passed an order accordingly and being aggrieved by that order the aggrieved party took the case before the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division in a very extensive judgment after discussing all the relevant cases of the English, Indian and Pakistani jurisdictions finally laid down the law on this point and in this case as a matter of fact, the Appellate Division did not allow any interest to the respondent, i.e., the contractor, and maintained the order of the trial Court. Therefore, Mr Hakim contends that though he does not dispute the principles laid down by the High Court Division in 45 DLR 712 but in the facts and circumstances of the present case, which is similar to that case, the appellant is not entitled to get any interest whatsoever. In this connection he also relies on two other decisions, namely, 7 BLC (AD) 97 and 55 DLR (AD) 139 and relying on the principles laid down in these cases he submitted that the trial Court taking a correct view of law, at least on this point, pronounced a correct judgment refusing to give any interest on the awarded sum. 

 9. Mr Rafiqul Islam Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, at the very outset raised a question of law as to the maintainability of the two appeals filed by the owner. Referring to the proviso to section 33 of the Act, which was incorporated in 1978 pursuant to the Law Reforms Ordinance, he submitted that since 1978 no application is entertain able under section 33 of the Act to set aside the award unless the applicant furnishes security to the satisfaction of the Court for the payment of such sum as awarded by the Arbitrator/Umpire or fulfils any other obligations by him under the award and in the instant case when they filed an application before the trial Court under section 33 of the Act and the objection under section 7 of the Act they had furnished a bank guarantee as security for the awarded amount but at the time of filing these appeals they have not deposited any amount in cash nor furnished any security to cover the awarded amount. Therefore, this offends the proviso to section 33 of the Act which is equally applicable to the appeal filed under section 39 (vi) of the Act against an order refusing to set aside the award and making the award a Rule of the Court under section 17 of the Act. To elaborate his submission he further submits that this proviso was added to the original section 33 pursuant to Ordinance 78 of 1978 for easy and speedy recovery of awarded amount in the event of making the award Rule of the Court. He further submits that in the past in arbitration matter after getting an award the party in whose favour award was given, even after making the award Rule of the Court, could not realise the money without initiating any execution case pursuant to the decree drawn under section 17 of the Act and to get rid of that situation and for speedy disposal of the matter this proviso has been added so that once the arbitration proceeding reaches its finality the party can easily realise the amount by withdrawing the security from the Court. The learned Advocate further, to fortify his argument on this point, submits that the expression "the Court" as defined in section 2(c) of the Act includes Appellate Court as has been held in the case reported in 16 DLR 260, Therefore, there is no scope for the appellants to escape the proviso in preferring the aforesaid appeals. The learned Advocate further, to elaborate his submission, submits that if a party is allowed to prefer an appeal without furnishing any security either in cash or in other form and the appeal is entertained and disposed of on merit that will cause miscarriage of justice to the innocent party inasmuch as in that case the appellant will get a benefit indirectly which he cannot get directly as at the initial stage when he challenges the validity or otherwise of the award at the trial Court he is under the legal obligation to furnish security for awarded amount but when the award is made Rule of the Court then in preferring an appeal if this provision is "relaxed, the appellant is given best of both the worlds, inasmuch as he has not only lost before the Arbitrator/Umpire but also lost before the trial Court and after losing before the arbitrator he is in a disadvantageous position when he calls in question the validity of the award before the trial Court but is in a better position when he takes up the matter before the appellate forum under section 39 of the Act and if this is allowed that would defeat the purpose of the legislation as introduced by the Ordinance in 1978 and run counter to the object of the Arbitration Act. He then contends that keeping the scheme and spirit of the legislation in mind and the definition as given in section 2(c), the word "Court" must be construed as widely as possible and that must include the appellate Court. The learned Advocate further submits that precisely this question came up before the Dhaka High Court in the case already cited and Hassan, J took the view that "the Court" as defined in section 2(c) of the Act includes appellate Court for the purpose of section 21 of the Act. 

 10. The second plank of attack made by Mr Miah is that in the facts and circumstances of the case and on the basis of materials on record it is crystal clear that the contractor is entitled to get compensation on claim No. 1 inasmuch as admittedly the owner could not make the land available to the contractor after execution of the contract and as a result they had to keep their men and material idle and unutilised for 42 days. It was the obligation of the owner to make all the lands available to the contractor after execution of the contract but the admitted position is that some portion of the land was not acquired at the time when the owner executed the instant contract and pursuant to the provisions of the contract the contractor had to mobilise his men and material and it appears that the owner being satisfied on scrutiny that on execution of the contract the contractor has taken appropriate steps to mobilise men and material the owner made the initial mobilisation payments. Mr Miah then submits that the contractor due to no fault of his rather but due to the fault of the owner the contractor had to keep a large number of labourers, i.e., 1000 labourers were kept idle and could not carry out the contractual work as the miscreants took over possession of the part of the land and therefore, the Executive Engineer vide his letter dated 10-10-94 addressed to the Deputy Commissioner, Nilphamari, requested him to take urgent measure to evict the miscreants from the project land and, basing on this letter, he submits that the admitted position is that the requisition and acquisition of the entire land for the project could not be completed by the appropriate agency on the date on which the contract was entered into between the parties and even after starting of the works some portion of the land was in occupation of the intruders for 42 days. As a result the contractor suffered loss in terms of money in paying the workers bill for subsistence allowance the account of which was datewise furnished to the Executive Engineer. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true in Article 4.01 of Part 11 of the contract document it is embodied that if there be delay in handing over the land by the owner to the contractor and if the contractor sustains a loss of time he will be entitled to get an extension of the contract time therefor but neither in clause 4.01 nor anywhere in the contract document it has been ever spelt out that for any breach committed by the owner the contractor will have no remedy under the law. Therefore, the contractor is entitled to get compensation on his claim for loss as sustained by his for no fault of them rather due to the fault and/or negligence of the owner, inasmuch as while executing the contract they had given a time-frame to the contractor within which they are to complete the entire project and in spite of incorporating such a stringent term in the contract the owner is oblivious of the fact that the project land had not yet been acquired by the Government and it was not handed over to them and this fact was within the knowledge of the owner when they executed the contract. To strengthen his submission on this point, the relies on the decision reported in 45 DLR 712 and submits that the contractor is entitled to get compensation though it was not specifically mentioned that the contractor will get any compensation therefor. The learned Advocate further submits that the said case was taken before the Appellate Division by the aggrieved party but they had not challenged the judgment on this point and the Appellate Division also did not reverse that finding. Therefore, Mr Miah contends that it is now well settled that if it is found that there is a breach of contract or breach of any terms of contract committed by a party the innocent party is, under the substantive law of the country, entitled to get compensation. 

 11. The next submission made by Mr Miah is in respect of the other claims. He submits that claim Nos. 2-9 raised by the contractor before the Arbitrator/Umpire emanated from the contract as a result of various breaches committed by the owner at various stages during the execution of the contract. Therefore, by no stretch of imagination it can be said that these claims are not covered by the contractual terms or outside the contractual obligation of the owner. In elaborating this point Mr Miah submits that during the course of execution of the contract a series of correspondences were made by the contractor with the owner and all these letters of both the parties were placed before the Arbitrators by the parties and both the Arbitrators taking into consideration the same found it difficult to agree with each other in the matter of claim and as a result they gave separate award whereupon the matter was taken before the Umpire and the Umpire on consideration of the materials on record ultimately concurred with the award given by Mr Luthfe Alam, the Arbitrator appointed by the contractor and disagreed with the award given by Mr Serajul Islam, the retired Additional Chief Engineer of the owner who was owner's arbitrator and gave the instant award. Mr Miah then submits that the findings arrived at by the Umpire are on consideration of the earlier two awards given by the two Arbitrators and also on consideration of the materials on record and therefore, by no stretch of imagination it can be said that, the instant award is defective on any count whatsoever inasmuch as the findings and decisions arrived at by the learned Umpire is borne out by the evidence and materials on record. He further contends that in an appeal filed under section 39 of the Act all that the Court is to see is that if the appellant has been able to bring his case within one of the three grounds as enunciated in section 30 of the Act so far it relates to Appeal No. 94 of 2004 and the trial Court in its turn on consideration of the materials and evidence on record rightly found that there is nothing on record to interfere with the award given by the Umpire and he has also observed that the appellant failed to substantiate the grounds taken by them before him and in that view of the matter the trial Court below rejected the application filed under section 33 of the Act and also rejected the objection filed under section 17 of the Act in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 202 of 2002 which has been subsequently re-numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 12 of 2003. Mr Miah then makes an additional submission on Appeal No. 66, of 2004 and submits that admittedly this is an appeal under section 17 of the Act where the scope to interfere with the impugned decree is very much limited and only on two counts the appellate Court can interfere with a decree which is drawn by the trial Court under section 17 after making the award Rule of the Court, i.e. if the appellant can show that the decree is either in excess of the award or not otherwise in accordance with the award. Mr Miah with regard to Appeal No. 66 of 2004 further submits that there is nothing on record to show that the decree is either in excess of the award or not otherwise in accordance with the award and in Appeal No. 66 of 2004 the grounds taken by the appellant does not show that they had taken any such ground in that appeal. Therefore, Appeal No. 66 of 2004 has, in any case, no legs to stand on as the appellants have miserably failed to bring the said appeal within the narrow alley as contemplated by section 17 of the Act. Mr Miah then submits that the owner very emphatically argued before this Court that by awarding compensation the Arbitrator/ Umpire acted beyond their jurisdiction and thereby misconducted the proceedings but no such ground was ever taken up by the owner in their rejoinder before the Arbitrator that no compensation could be paid in the instant case for loss of time nor before the trial Court the said stand was taken and, as such, the owner cannot urge such a question before this Court for the first time which they did neither urge or take up either before the Arbitrator/Umpire or before the trial Court inasmuch as the settled position of law is that a point which was not urged before, the Court cannot be taken up for the first time before this Court in appeal and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in 50 DLR (AD) 63. 

 12. Mr Rafiqul Islam Miah, the learned Advocate, then diverted his attention to his own appeal and submits that in the instant case the contractor claimed interest before the Arbitrator/Umpire and also before the trial Court and the Umpire in entertaining the claims of the contractor also awarded interest on the principal sum @ 10% pendente lite but the trial Court absolutely on misconception of facts and law refused to maintain the interest as given by the Umpire on the mistaken idea that the contractor is not entitled to get any interest in the instant case as admittedly the contractor is not a banking company and it is only a banking company which deals with money lending that is entitled to get an order of interest in the event of breach committed by its customers. Mr Miah very emphatically and with all the force that he could command submitted that this observation is absolutely erroneous and contrary to the principles of law. Mr Miah further submits that it would be unjust and inequitable if the Court refuses to pass an order of interest in a case where, as a matter of fact, it is found that the money is due from the other party and the other party is deliberately and intentionally withholding the payment of the said money. Mr Miah to elaborate his submission further submits that after getting the award it was made Rule of the Court on 16-10-2003 and the award was given by the Umpire on 14-9-2002 and the Arbitration notices were served on 1-10-96 and the first set of Arbitrators entered into reference on 14-10-1996 and after the elapse of 3 years when they were removed by the Court the present set of Arbitrators entered the reference on 21-4-2001 and it reached its finality after making of the award Rule of the Court on 16-10-2003. The contract work was completed on 14-12-1995. Therefore, in the event of successful termination of the case in favour of the contractor they will be, in fact, worse off if no interest is given to them, inasmuch as we live in a time where inflation is the order of the day throughout the world and the money value decreases every year due to the inflationary trend in the economy. Therefore, if at the end of the day the contractor wins the case and no interest is awarded pendente lite on the sum awarded the contractor will walk out of the Court with empty pocket even if he wins the case because the volume of inflation in the meantime has eaten up the entire sum awarded by the Umpire and this aspect of the inflationary trend in the money market in every country of the world has been taken note of by all the superior Courts in every jurisdiction. Mr Miah relying on the decision reported in 46 DLR (AD) 97 submits that the scope of payment of interest on an award is finally settled by our Appellate Division in that case and the majority view is that in the absence of any stipulation in the contract itself as to the payment of interest the Arbitrator/Umpire can award interest from the date of entering into the reference till the date of making the award and it is only in a case if there is a stipulation in the contract itself that the Arbitrator will be entitled to pass an order of interest for the pre-reference period in that case only the Arbitral Tribunal can pass an order for interest for the pre-reference period. It is also well settled that it is only the Court which is authorised by law to pass an order for interest pendente lite pursuant to the provision of section 29 of the Act and it is the Court and Court only which can pass an order of interest for the period from the date of making the award Rule of the Court till the date of realisation of the decretal amount. Mr Miah to fortify his submission on the point of interest also relied on some of the decisions of the Indian Supreme Court and of English Jurisdiction and some of those cases have been considered by the Appellate Division in 46 DLR. Mr Miah heavily relied on the observation of Lord Denning given in Chandry's case of the Court of Appeal of England and that observation has been noticed by the High Court Division in 45 DLR and the Appellate Division in 46 DLR case. 

 13. Mr Miah submits that in the instant case as per contract the money was due in 1995 and that payment is still being withheld by the owner. Even if the contractor wins the case in this Court it can be said that the matter will not end here. The other party will go to the Appellate Division and that will take further time to settle the matter and after a period of 15 years if the contractor at long last wins the case and he is simply given the awarded amount without any interest he will not only be financially worse off but the awarded amount will come to a negative figure due to inflationary trend that prevailed over in the money market for the last 15 years. He further contends that in the interest of justice and fair play equity demands that in such a case the innocent party should be given the interest to set off the loss sustained by him due to the inflationary trend in the present-day economy. Mr Miah further submits that the admitted posit-ion is that the contractor has claimed interest before the Arbitrator though they have not made any factual statement that to carry out the contract they have taken loan from the National Bank but when the payment was delayed by the owner the contractor vide their letter dated 3-4-1996 written to the Superintending Engineer of the owner stated that the contractor has taken a loan from the National Bank for the purpose of this contract and the Umpire taking into consideration this material aspect along with the other materials awarded interest to the contractor but the trial Court without considering these materials and taking an erroneous view of law most illegally refused to give interest. More so, when papers were produced before the Arbitrator/Umpire to show that interest is being charged on their account by the bank for non-payment of outstanding dues. Therefore, in a case like this where the principal amount remains outstanding for a long time it is bound to cause hardship of the highest magnitude to the contractor if interest is refused to him in an economic system where uncontrolled inflation prevails in the market. 

 14. Mr Miah finally submitted that the cases relied on by the appellants have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case inasmuch as the facts of those cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case. The learned Advocate further submits that the case reported in AIR 2003 (SC) 2629 on an ultimate analysis does not support the owner rather it supports the contractor, inasmuch as on an analysis of the contractual terms it becomes clear and obvious that the Umpire rightly awarded the compensation and interest on the principal amount. 

 15. Mr AKM Abdul Hakim, the learned Advocate appearing for the owner, in reply on the point of maintainability of the appeals, submitted that the cases cited and relied on by the contractor, namely, the cases reported in 49 DLR 335 and 54 DLR 161 have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, inasmuch as in those cases at the time of filing application under section 33 of the Act no security at all was furnished by the objector although since 1978 it is mandatory and on that ground the application filed by the objectors were rejected by the trial Court which was upheld by this Court in an appeal but in the instant case the owner at the time of filing of the application under section 33 of the Act furnished proper security before the trial Court and they did not furnish any security at the time of presentation of the Memo of Appeal as it is not required by law. The learned Advocate submits that the provision for preferring appeal is provided by section 39(vi) which is applicable in the instant case and this section does not say that the appellant shall have to furnish any security covering the amount of the award at the time of filing of the appeal. The learned Advocate further submits that besides it is also now well settled that the Court defined in section 2(c) of the Act does not include the appellate Court. Therefore, the proviso which is appended to section 33 of the Act cannot be stretched too far to apply to section 39 of the Act. Therefore, it was not the legal requirement on the part of the owner to furnish any kind of security at the time of filing of the appeals, he contends. In support of his contention he relies on the cases reported in AIR 1947 Calcutta 93 and 49 DLR 113. 

 17. We have studied these cases as best as we could and it appears to us, in fact, none of the decisions help either of the parties. In the cases reported in 49 DLR 335 and 54 DLR 161 the admitted position is that the party who filed the application under section 33 did not furnish any security at the time of filing of the application. Therefore, these were caught by the mischief of the proviso to section 33. Here it may be stated that the similar question came up for consideration before another bench of this Court which is reported in 1988 BLD 369 wherein it was held that the provisions for deposit contemplated under the law is a condition precedent for entertaining of an application challenging the award and without the deposit it is to be construed, that there was no application in the eye of law and in that case deposit was made during the pendency of the case but that also was found not to be sufficient to rectify the mischief committed by the party by omitting to deposit the amount along with the application and this view was taken by a Division Bench of this Court as the language of the proviso is mandatory. Therefore, in 49 DLR 335 and 54 DLR 161 the trial Court rejected the applications filed by the objector as no deposit was made and in both the cases the objectors went in appeal to the High Court Division and the High Court Division upheld the finding of the trial Court holding that as the mandatory provision of deposit was not complied with by the objector at the time of filing of the application they had, in the eye of law, no existence at all and, as such, they were rejected outright by the trial Court and in that view of the matter the appeal was also not competent for non-compliance with the mandatory provision of law. 

 18. The case reported in 49 DLR 113 is also not relevant for the issue raised in this case inasmuch as in that case the issue was, whether the undertaking given by the Chairman on behalf of the Water Development Board would be treated as a security within the meaning of the proviso to section 33 of the Act and on an analysis of the law the Court held that since the undertaking given by the Chairman on behalf of the Water Development Board was also endorsed by the Members of the Board, the Court found that this was sufficient compliance with the proviso appended to section 33 of the Act. In the instant case admitted position is that security was furnished before the trial Court and admittedly no security has been furnished before this Court at the time of presentation of the Memo of Appeal. Therefore, pertinent question which calls for determination now is to see whether the provision for furnishing security is also applicable in case of appeal. 

 19. In order to appreciate, the legal aspects involved in this case it would be useful if we trace the history of the law of Arbitration in this Sub-continent and the entire scheme of the Act. 

 21. In regard to appeals, section 358 provided that "the appellate Court shall have all the like powers in regard to the granting of time, adjourning the hearing of the suit, examining the parties or their pleaders, and awarding costs, or otherwise as are hereinbefore contained in regard to Courts of original jurisdiction." This section was repealed by section 1 of Act 23 of 1881, but section 37 of that Act provided that, "Unless when otherwise provided, the appellate Court shall have the same powers in cases of appeals which are vested in the Courts of original jurisdiction in respect to original suits." 

 24. Act 10 of 1877 was repealed by Act 14 of 1882. The provisions relating to arbitration were similar to those made in the previous Act, vide sections 506 to 526. The provisions of section 582 of Act 10 of 1877 were incorporated in section 582 of the Code of 1882. By this time it was well settled that an appellate Court with the consent of parties could refer a case to arbitration. See 'In re Sangaralingam Pillai', 3 Mad 78 (E). 

 (a) to determine a case finally, 

 (b) to remand a case, 

 28. When the Arbitration Act of 1940 was enacted, the law relating to arbitration was to be found mainly in the Second Schedule of the Civil Procedure Code and in the Indian Arbitration Act of 1899. These provisions were repealed and a consolidated Act was passed to deal with the entire law relating to arbitration. The preamble to the Act shows that it is a consolidating and amending Act. The scheme of the Act is this: Chapter II deals with arbitration without intervention of the Court. This chapter contains sections 3 to 19. It is clear that this chapter deals with a case in which there is no suit pending and parties have agreed to refer their differences to arbitration and an award is also made without the intervention of a Court. Chapter III deals with arbitration with the intervention of the Court where no suit is pending. In other words, where there is an arbitration agreement, but where no award has been made, the agreement may be filed in Court by means of an application. Such application will be registered as a suit and then the matter will be referred to arbitrators. Chapter IV, which consists of sections 21 to 25, deals with arbitration in pending suits. Parties may apply to the Court to have the suit or any issue therein referred to arbitration and thereafter the other provisions relating to arbitration shall be followed. Then there are general provisions which apply to all the three kinds of arbitration proceedings mentioned in Chapters II, III and IV. 

 33. It is by now clear that initially arbitration proceedings were carried on under the regulation. Then the field was governed by the Code since 1859 and the Indian Arbitration Act of 1899. These provisions were repealed and a consolidated Act in the form of Arbitration Act, 1940 was enacted. After the enactment of the 1940 Act there has been divergence of opinion in India at the High Court level. The Calcutta View has been expressed in AIR 1947 Cal 93 wherein it was held that the term "Court" as defined in the Act does not include an appellate Court. Similarly, there appears to be a divergence of opinion in the Allahabad High Court. In the case reported in AIR 1947 All 304, it was held that an appellate Court had no power to make reference to arbitration in respect of the subject matter of an appeal pending before it. It was also interpreted that the word 'suit' in section 2 had the mere technical and restricted meaning in a proceeding instituted in a Court of first instance. But in a later case, the Allahabad High Court, i.e., the case reported in AIR 1948 All 443 a contrary view was taken. There it was held that it was not necessary to give such a restricted meaning to the word 'suit' in section 21 and their Lordships expressed the opinion that the term would not exclude executing proceedings or appeals before a civil Court. Again, in the case reported in AIR 1953 All 9, the view expressed in AIR 1948 All 443 was approved by a Full Bench of the said Court. The view expressed by the Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court has been followed by Patna High Court, Madras High Court and Rajasthan High Court. See AIR 1954 Pat 106, AIR 1955 Mad 693 and AIR 1957 Raj 278. The Patna case was also followed by the Dacca High Court in the case reported in 16 DLR 260 = PLD 1966 Dacca 54 to hold that the term 'Court' included the appellate Court as well. 

 34. The controversy has, however, been finally set at rest in India by the Indian Supreme Court in the case reported in AIR 1960 SC 307. There the Indian Supreme Court held that "In considering this question it should be relevant and material to take notice of the fact that prior to the passing of the Act in 1940 the long-standing practice of Indian Court was to refer to arbitration disputes pending before the appellate Court between the respective parties to the appeals. If the object of enacting section 21 was to prohibit such reference at the appellate stage it would, as the High Court has observed, bring a revolution in the existing practice. Was such a revolution really intended? Having regard to the fact that the words used in section 21 are substantially the same as those used in section 11, paragraph 1 of the earlier Code, it would be difficult to sustain the plea that the enactment of section 21 was intended to bring about such a violent departure from the existing practice. If that had been the intention of the Legislature it would have made appropriate changes in the words used in section 21. Therefore, the word 'Court' cannot be interpreted to mean only the trial Court as contended by the appellants, similarly, the word 'suit' cannot be construed in the narrow sense of meaning only the suit and not an appeal. In our opinion, 'Court' in section 21 includes the appellate Court proceedings before which are generally recognised as continuation of the suit and the word "suit" will include such appellate proceedings. We may add that whereas section 41 of the Act is consistent with this view no other section militates against it. 

 42. By the Law Reforms Ordinance, i.e., Ordinance No. 49 of 1978, a proviso has been added to the original section 33 which now provides for furnishing sufficient security to the satisfaction of the Court for payment of awarded sum or for the fulfilment of any other obligation along with the application filed under section 33 of the Act and this provision is a mandatory one and non-compliance with the proviso disentitles the applicant to get his application heard by the Court on merit. In the instant case, in compliance with the said proviso the owner has furnished necessary security before the trial Court but admittedly while preferring the appeals they have not filed any security whatsoever to cover the liability of the appellants. In such background, Mr Miah has raised the question of maintainability of the appeals for non-depositing the awarded amount or any security for the same along with the memorandum of appeal. We have already noted that appeal No. 66 of 2004 is an appeal under section 17 of the Act whereas appeal No. 94 of 2004 is an appeal under section 39(1)(vi) of the Act. Neither in section 17 nor in section 39 there is any express stipulation that the aggrieved party if prefers appeal has to furnish security to the extent of the amount awarded by the Arbitrator/Umpire as the case may be. To our knowledge this is the first case in which this question has come up for consideration by this Division. We have already indicated that the 49 DLR case and 54 DLR case are, in fact, not exactly on the point inasmuch as in those cases the appeals were found incompetent as the appellant did not, as a matter of fact, furnish any security before the trial Court at the time of filing of the application under section 33 of the Act. Therefore, it needs an interpretation as to whether the proviso appended to section 33 of the Act can be stretched to or read into the provisions of the aforesaid two sections of the Act. In this connection, we must bear in mind that in 1978 this provision was incorporated in the Act for the first time so that the awardee after the making of the award can easily and speedily recover the amount awarded to him after rejection of the objection filed under section 33 of the Act. We have already held that 'Court' for the purpose of the Arbitration Act as defined in section 2(c) of the Act also includes an appellate Court including the High Court Division. Though in section 39 or in section 17 there is no provision of furnishing of any security nevertheless, if the defaulting party after losing in two Courts is allowed to file an appeal without depositing the amount in question then it would lead to a situation where the wrongdoer will get best of both the worlds. It is also inequitable and unjust in any view inasmuch as the aggrieved party i.e. the losing party, requires to file an objection after furnishing the security before the trial Court and then after losing before the trial Court if he is allowed to prefer an appeal without furnishing any security to cover his liability he would be better off after losing before two forums and the innocent party will be worse off for no fault of his and the real purpose of the law would be defeated and frustrated. Therefore, we are of the opinion that in the interest of justice and equity the provision for deposit as contained in the proviso of section 33 of the Act must be extended to and read into the provisions as contained either in section 17 or section 39 of the Act, otherwise the amendment would become futile and meaningless and the defaulting party would be given the upper hand even after losing before two forums. Therefore, we have no hesitation in holding that in filing an appeal either under section 17 or 39(1)(vi) of the Act the appellant must deposit the awarded amount or furnish necessary security to the satisfaction of the appellate Court. It would be preposterous to think that it was the intention of the Parliament that in filing an application under section 33 of the Act the aggrieved party will have to deposit the awarded amount but after losing both before the Arbitrator and the trial Court he will not be required to deposit any such amount before the appellate Court. If this interpretation is accepted it will not only lead to a blind alley but will also equally lead to an absurd proposition where the wrongdoer will be better off at the cost of the innocent party. Thus, we find that the First Appeal No. 66 of 2004 and FMA No. 94 of 2004 are incompetent and not maintainable for non-deposit of the awarded amount or any other sufficient security to cover it up. 

 43. These are first appeals and in these appeals we have heard both the parties at length on merit as well. Therefore, we would also like to touch the merits of the aforesaid two appeals. Mr AKM Abdul Hakim the learned Advocate relying on the decisions reported in (1991) 4 SCC 93, 57 DLR 626, (1999) 8 SCC 122 and AIR 2003. (SC) 2629, repeatedly urged before us that the award in question is bad in law and the trial Court most illegally made the same Rule of the Court and therefore, both the learned umpire as well as the trial Court lost sight of an important and material question of law, that the Arbitrator/Umpire in the instant case committed jurisdictional error and therefore, the award made by them is a nullity in the eye of law. Therefore, there was no scope for the trial Court to make it a Rule of the Court. We have studied the aforesaid decisions and Mr Rafiqul Islam Miah also did not at any stage of the hearing doubt the soundness of the principles laid down in those decisions but he submitted that in the facts and circumstances of this case those cases have no manner of application. In 57 DLR case it has been laid down that in any Arbitration proceeding the agreement is the foundation and nobody disputes this proposition. Here the parties are at loggerheads as to the scope of the arbitration. According to Mr Hakim, the arbitration clause does not authorise the arbitrator/umpire to award compensation for loss of time for non-handing over the entire land to the contractor in time. As opposed to this, Mr Miah contends that the arbitration clause is wide enough to authorise the arbitrator/umpire to award compensation and damages for loss caused to the contractor due to the fault/negligence of the owner. In this connection, it is interesting to note that even the owner did not raise this question before the arbitrator/ umpire. It further appears that the owner also did not take such specific ground even before the lower Court. Be that as it may, since it is a question of law of great importance we would like to address the question first Mr Hakim has strenuously argued before us about the jurisdictional error committed by the arbitrator/umpire. His straightforward contention is that in the present case the contractor's claim is for damage and compensation but in the agreement there is no provision for claiming damage and compensation by the contractor from the owner. Thus, he vehemently urged before us that the arbitrator/umpire acted beyond jurisdiction and passed the award beyond the limit of the scope of the agreement. On this point he first relied on the case of Associated Engineering Co. reported in (1991) 4 SCC 93. In this case the Indian Supreme Court laid down the following three principles of law, namely, that an arbitrator cannot act arbitrarily, irrationally, capriciously or independently of the contract. His sole function is to arbitrate in terms of the contract. He has no power apart from the power parties have given him under the contract. If he has travelled outside bounds of the contract, he has acted without jurisdiction; an arbitrator who acts in manifest disregard of the contract acts without jurisdiction. His authority is derived from the contract and is governed by the Arbitration Act and a dispute as to jurisdiction of the arbitrator is not a dispute within the award but one which has to be decided outside the award. An umpire or arbitrator cannot widen his jurisdiction by deciding a question not referred to him by the parties or by deciding a question otherwise than in accordance with the contract and if he wanders outside the contract or deals with matters not allotted to him he commits a jurisdictional error and such error not only amounts to misconduct but also vitiates the award. In fact, same principles have been reiterated by the Indian. Supreme Court in the case reported in (1999) 8 SCC wherein the Indian Supreme Court in the given facts of that case observed that when the question of jurisdictional error is raised before the Court the Court has to decide that issue after examining the terms of the contract and if any terms of the contract expressly prohibits the Arbitrator to pass an award on a specific item in such case if an award is given on that item that would no doubt, tantamount to jurisdictional error or which is commonly known as judicial misconduct and any such award would be without jurisdiction. The other recent case is the case reported in AIR 2003(SC) 2629 which has been relied on by Mr Hakim. This case is under the new Indian law, i.e., Arbitration and Conciliation Act, (Act 26 of 1996). In the new Act, Court is empowered to set aside an award of arbitral Tribunal. In interpreting the scope of this section the Indian Supreme Court, in the light of the provisions of the new Act, laid down that if the award is contrary to the substantive provisions of law or the provisions of the Act or against the terms of the contract, it would be patently illegal which could be interfered with under section 34 (which is parallel to sections 30 and 33 of 1940 Act). However, such failure of procedure should be patent affirming rights of the parties. In paragraph No. 75 the Court amongst others, held that the Court can set aside the arbitral award under section 34(2) Of the Act if the party making the application furnishes proof that the arbitral award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration or it contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration. In this judgment also the Indian Supreme Court has reiterated principles as valid law which they had laid down in the earlier two decisions. 

 44. Now, in the background of these settled principles, let us see if the contract in question bars the arbitration proceeding which has been initiated by the parties. In the new law, i.e., the Arbitration Act, 2001, the arbitrators have been invested with the powers to examine the question as to whether they are competent to proceed with the arbitration or the agreement in question, in fact, is an agreement for arbitration. But in the earlier law, i.e., 1940 Act, this authority was not vested in the Arbitrator rather this power was given to the Court. Be that as it may, from the materials and evidence on record we do not find any material which shows that at any point of time before the making of the award either of the parties raised this question before the Arbitrator. Rather, the main and substantial argument of the appellants at the Arbitration stage was that this Arbitration proceeding is incompetent and not maintainable in view of the fact that the contractor had given undertaking in writing before the settlement of the final bill to the competent authority stating that henceforth they will not come up with any further claim in respect of the contract in question and that contention raised by the appellant before the Arbitrator has been negatived by the Umpire on the basis of evidence and materials on record and that finding of the Umpire has also been confirmed by the trial Court on the basis of the materials and evidence on record. Therefore, it was not the case of the appellants before the arbitrator that the terms do not allow the Arbitrator to go for arbitration as the agreement does not provide for such arbitration, rather it was the stand that the arbitration is incompetent in view of the undertaking given by the contractor to the owner. However, before the trial Court halfheartedly they tried to say that in conducting the Arbitration proceeding the Arbitrator/Umpire committed jurisdictional error and that contention of the appellants have also been negatived by the trial Court as well. Be that as it may, this is a question of law and we are of the view that a question of law can be raised at any stage of the proceeding although it was not raised in clear terms at the earlier stage, This is also well settled that it is never too late to set aside an order which has been passed without jurisdiction. Pakistan Supreme Court in the case reported in PLD 1958 (SC) 201 observed that the order which is a nullity must be removed, since it becomes a precedent. Therefore, it enjoins a duty upon us to decide the issue in or ie way or the other. The bone of contention of Mr Hakim is that Article 4 of Part II of Firsisty relates to the availability of lands. It has been laid down in Article 4.01 that the owner shall furnish the lands upon which the work is to be done. If the contractor sustains a loss of time by delay in the owner's furnishing lands or easements, he is entitled to an extension of contract time there for Relying on this and on the fact that this project was financed by Saudi grant, it was submitted that that's why in the event of failure to furnish the lands in time, the contractor was entitled to extension of time there for and nowhere in the contract it has been expressly provided that if there is any breach committed by the owner the contractor will be entitled to get any compensation for such breach. Therefore, in awarding compensation in respect of claim No.1 the Arbitrators traveled beyond their jurisdiction. As against that, Mr Miah, on the other hand, relied on the decision reported in 45 DLR 712 where compensation was awarded to a party for the breach committed by the other. Mr Hakim has tried to distinguish that case from the present case on facts. 

 (a) that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself or the proceedings; 

 46. Thus, it was held in the case reported in 20 DLR 469 that it is not open to the appellant to ask the appellate Court to go into the details of the claim and counterclaim or to re-assess the question as if this was a Court of appeal from a decision of a Civil Court in its ordinary jurisdiction. It was further observed that the only point of some seriousness which arose in that case was whether the Arbitrator/ Umpire were guilty of legal/jurisdictional misconduct in giving the award in a lump-sum without specifying their decision on each item which included compensation. It is to be noted that the Arbitrator/Umpire found that there was a breach of contract committed by the owner. So, the pertinent question raised is, if in such situation the Arbitrator is entitled in law to award compensation/damages against the defaulting party. The same question also came up before this Division in 45 DLR's case reported at page 712 and there also contention was raised that no compensation can be awarded by the Arbitrator /Umpire in the absence of any specific provision contained in the agreement itself and that contention was negatived by this Division and that case was also taken by the owner to the Appellate Division but before the Appellate Division they had given a go-bye to this contention and concentrated their case only on the question of awarding of interest by the Arbitrator. The agreement contained an arbitration clause to the effect any dispute of claims which cannot be amicably settled by negotiation between the contractor and the employer shall be settled by arbitration in accordance with the laws for arbitration effective in Bangladesh. The contractor claimed compensation for loss sustained by them for stoppage of work for 47 days. The owner denied the claim as the stoppage of work was not at their instance and also on the ground that the agreement does not provide for compensation for loss due to such stoppage of work. The contention was negatived by the arbitrator and the award so far it relates to compensation was made a Rule of the Court. In that case it was held by this Division that the expression "any dispute" appearing in the arbitration clause includes in the expression "all differences" and thus upheld the award for compensation. 

 47. In the present case the arbitration clause is much wider. It states "if any dispute or difference of any kind whatsoever shall arise between the owner/ the Engineer and the contractor in connection with or arising out of the contract  " shall be resolved through arbitration as per Article 15.02. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we have no hesitation to hold that in awarding compensation for loss sustained by the contractor on account of non-availability of lands, the arbitrator acted within their jurisdiction. More so when there is no prohibition clause in the contract that the contractor will not get any compensation for loss sustained due to the fault of the owner. In (1991) 4 SCC case all that the Indian Supreme Court has said is that in awarding a compensation the Court has to examine the terms of the contract and see if the arbitrator arbitrated in terms of the contract and in that case it was found, as a matter of fact, that the umpire out stepped the confines of the contract and the error arose not by misreading or misconstruing or misunderstanding the contract and in (1999) 8 SCC Case it has been further held that in the event of prohibition contained in an agreement as to the payment of compensation the Arbitrators cannot award compensation. Award passed in disregard of express terms of the contract would amount to jurisdictional error. So is the view expressed by the Indian Supreme Court in the case reported in AIR 2003. Mr Miah does not dispute the proposition of law laid down by the Indian Supreme Court in those cases but submits that the facts of those cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case. In those cases it was found on materials on record that the arbitrator had no authority to award compensation as by express terms of the contract such payment of compensation was prohibited but in the instant case there is no such prohibition. We have gone through the evidence on record furnished by the parties before the Arbitrators, very carefully examined the award given by the Umpire and the impugned judgment and we are of the opinion that there is no prohibition clause in the agreement that in the event of breach committed by the owner no compensation or damages can be awarded by the Arbitrator/Umpire. Here on the facts we find that the agreement does not prohibit the Arbitrator to award any compensation in the event of breach committed by either party. We have already held that the Umpire and the lower Court rightly found that there is breach of contract committed by the owner. 

 48. Now the question that arises is what legal incidence would follow from such a breach in the absence of any stipulation that compensation cannot be awarded for any breach committed by either party. We have already noted that no such clause is incorporated in the contract and rightly did not do so because of sections 73 and 74 of the Contract Act. Section 73 of the Contract Act provides for damages in the event of committal of breach of contract and the principle, which is universally followed by all the Courts, is the doctrine of restitutio in integram which really means that Court will endeavour to put the parties as equally as possible to the position/ situation had there been no breach of contract. Therefore, compensation naturally and automatically follows from any breach of contract and the liability for breach of contract can be restricted either by incorporating a penalty clause or liquidated damage clause in the contract itself which has been provided for by section 74 of the Contract Act. In the instant case there is no such clause. Therefore, once it was found by the Umpire that there has been breach committed by the owner on more than one count, i.e. in respect of all the claims, the Umpire had to resolve the dispute in the light of the substantive law of the country which is the law of contract as embodied in section 73 of the Act and that aspect of law has been very clearly considered and discussed by the Indian Supreme Court in the case reported in AIR 2003 SC 2629 and the Indian Supreme Court in that case held that if an award is pronounced in derogation of or contrary to the substantive law of the country the award would be knocked down as contrary to public policy or contrary to law. In the instant case the Umpire rightly awarded compensation to militate the loss suffered by the contractor and the contractor is entitled to it in the facts and circumstances of the case. Mr Hakim in the course of his argument tried to characterise the contract as a contract of special type in view of the fact that the Saudi Development Grant would provide the fund for the project. This, in our view, does not make the contract a special contract. It is clear that the contract is in between the Bangladesh Water Development Board and the Titas Prokoushali and if any breach is committed by either party the innocent party will be entitled to damages in accordance with law and it is immaterial who provides the fund. The moot question is, whether there is a breach and we have no hesitation in answering the question in the affirmative and we do not find any illegality whatsoever in the award on that count because otherwise an innocent party will be left without any remedy and the defaulting party will have best of both the worlds. If we uphold the contention of Mr Hakim it would lead us to a blind alley which eventually will lead us to an absurd legal proposition where the weaker and the innocent party will be left with no remedy whereas the stronger and the defaulting party will have the upper hand in the matter. That kind of situation cannot prevail in any civilised society. Therefore, the source of fund is absolutely irrelevant so far it relates to the present issue and we do not find any substance or material on record to classify the contract other that a contract as known in the Contract Act within the meaning of section 2 of the said Act. So, this disposes of the contention so far it relates to the award of compensation by the Umpire and upholding the same by the trial Court and in view of the materials and evidence on record and discussions made aforesaid the awarding of compensation made by the Umpire does not amount to jurisdictional error in the instant case and the cases cited and relied on by Mr Hakim do not, in fact, help him. We have examined the grounds that were taken by the appellants. before the trial Court and substantially the self-same grounds are reproduced before this Court in the memo of appeal wherein they have indirectly taken a ground on jurisdictional error also which was not so clearly argued before the Courts below as has been done by Mr Hakim before us but we have already assigned reasons for our inability to see eye to eye with him on this point. 

 49. Now let us advert to the appeal filed by the contractor, i.e. Appeal No. 10 of 2005. It is found as a matter of fact that the contractor claimed interest before the Arbitrator/ Umpire and the Umpire at the time of making the award granted interest pendente lite, i.e., till realisation of the awarded amount, but while making the award a Rule of the Court the learned trial Court negatived all the contentions raised , by the respondents yet refused to maintain the order of the Umpire so far it relates to interest and refused to grant interest only and solely on the ground that the contractor is not entitled to any interest in the instant case as it is not a banking company. The trial Court refused to grant interest only on this ground. At one point of time there was some confusion on this point. Now the law has been finally settled by our Appellate Division in the case reported in 46 DLR (AD) 97. In this case the controversy on point of interest has been finally set at rest by our Appellate Division. So far it relates to payment of interest it has been divided into three segments—pre-reference interest, interest for the period under reference and interest for the post-reference period. So far it relates to the pre-reference interest law is that Arbitrator can award interest, for pre-reference period if the agreement so provides and the party claims the interest accordingly before the Arbitrator. The Arbitrator in any case notwithstanding any provision contained in the Arbitration agreement can award interest for the period under reference provided the party claims for such interest or even if the Arbitrator finds it reasonable to award interest. But so far it relates to the post-reference period the majority view which governs the field is that the Arbitrator has no authority whatsoever to make an order for interest for the post-reference period and it is only the Court which can pass such an order in the fitness of things pursuant to the provisions of section 29 of the Act. Therefore, the impugned order so far it relates to striking down the interest from the date of making the award till the date of realisation per se does not appear to be illegal. In this connection we may recall that in that case the trial Court refused interest and this Division granted interest which was reversed by the Appellate Division. We have very carefully studied the case of the 46 DLR and the Appellate Division after considering all the leading decisions of the Sub-continent as well as of the English jurisdiction and American jurisdiction in their wisdom did not find it sound and safe to leave the question of interest in the hands of the Arbitrator and was firmly inclined to leave the matter to the Court and they had reversed the order of the High Court Division on point of interest only on the ground that it is the Court which is authorised to take an order for pendente lite interest and since the trial Court has not awarded any interest they have upheld that decision. There is no indication in this judgment except as stated above why their Lordships were led to such a stand or what very fact/facts heavily weighed in their minds in not upholding the order of interest granted by this Division. Their Lordships have discussed the case of English Jurisdiction including Chandry's case and observed that Lord Denning, MR is well known for his progressive ideas which sometimes appear to be on the verge of revolutionary changes of law, was all along holding the view that an Arbitrator has got full discretion to award interest on the sum found by him as due but not paid in time and that the Arbitrator was not bound by the old Rules and practice followed by the juries. The Appellate Division also noted that Lord Denning was also of the view that the Arbitrator got power to award interest on the ground of equity, justice, fairness and good conscience. Taking into consideration these aspects, however, their Lordships in the given facts and circumstances of that case was not inclined to uphold the order of interest passed by this Division. The question of interest came up in various cases and in a society where inflation is the order of the day, where money loses its value every day, it needs serious consideration by the Court to see if in a case it is found as a matter of fact that the plaintiff is entitled to get money due from the defendant and the defendant is withholding it deliberately and without any valid reason, the defendant should be saddled with interest so as to reduce the loss in real terms sustained by the plaintiff over the years due to inflationary trend in the country. This aspect of the case was considered by Lord Denning in the case of Techno-impex v Gebr van Weelde BV, reported in (1981) 2 All England Law Reports 672 wherein Lord Denning observed: 

 50. Similar view was taken by Lord Denning in some earlier cases also including Finnix Case (Lloyd's Law Report, 1974, Volume-1) Thus the principle propounded by Lord Denning is that when a creditor is deprived of the use of his money he should be compensated for the deprivation, whether it is called interest, compensation or damage. 

 51. Ours is also a society where inflation is of high magnitude. Money deprecates day to day. The trend of inflation in our economy is always rising without any effective control. We can take judicial notice of this fact. In this background Mr Miah submitted that if at the end of the day the money is found due from the respondents and the contractor is not awarded any interest pendente lite, even by winning the case, they will be worse off and walk out of this Court with empty hands because in real terms they will not get any benefit at all. This case was started in 1996 and the award was given on 14-9-2002 for Taka one crore and odd along with the interest @ 10% per annum till realisation. If at the end of the day the award is confirmed by this Court and no interest is awarded on the decretal sum even by winning the case the contractor will be much worse off than they were on the day when the award was made Rule of the Court and /or when the award was made by the Umpire. We have already indicated that during the period under consideration the inflation is persisting. Even if the order of interest is maintained then also the contractor will, in fact, be worse off in real terms, Thus, non-allowing of interest will cause immense economic hardship to the contractor and they will walk out of the Court head down whereas the breaker of law would be better off which offends the principles of equity justice, fairplay and good conscience. 

 52. In an economy where inflationary trend pervades year after year without any abatement, money circulation increases disproportionately and people as a whole suffer from the devaluation of money, it would be inequitable not to grant interest on the awarded sum. In the instant case if the decree is upheld without awarding any interest the contractor will be worse off and walk out of the Court room not only with a broken heart but also with utter frustration that they live in a country where a party by winning a case in a Court of law becomes worse off and the legal system fails to redress their genuine grievance and if this be the trend the people in general and litigants in particular will lose faith in the Courts of law. In an economy where inflation is the order of the day the Court would like to place the innocent party to the position where he would have been had there been no breach of contract. 'Thus, an attempt must be made to reduce the gap as far as possible by awarding interest otherwise the rationals behind section 73 of the Contract Act will evaporate and will become a hollow word of law. Equity must prevail. Therefore, the Court of law must do what they could do. In the instant case in the given facts and circumstances it appears to us that if no interest is awarded on the decretal amount in the event of affirmation of the decree the sufferings of the contractor will not be remedied to a great extent. Therefore, justice and equity demands that if the decree is affirmed it should be followed by awarding of interest on the decretal amount. We are in full agreement with the observation given by Lord Denning in Techno Impex case and reiterate his sentiment and would be inclined to award interest if ultimately the decree is upheld. We have already noted that in 46 DLR their Lordships of the Appellate Division reversed the decision of this Division so far it relates to giving of interest in the facts and circumstances of that case and the facts of the instant case is quite distinguishable. 

 53. We have studied the case to the best of our ability. We find that besides laying down the principles relating to payment of interest their Lordships did not explain the reason what actually prompted them to arrive at such a decision save and except that the trial Court did not award any interest and the Appellate Division upheld the same which leads us to the conclusion that their Lordships of the Appellate Division, in the facts and circumstances of that case, was finally convinced that in that case the awardee failed to properly make out a case for interest pendente lite. It is well known and well settled that a principle of law laid down in a case is substantially and essentially dependent on the facts of each case and in the facts and circumstances of that case it was found to be fit by their Lordships of the Appellate Division not to award any interest. We have carefully examined all the materials and evidence on record and the award given by the Umpire and the two other Arbitrators and we do not find any cogent reason for refusing the interest to the contractor. From the impugned judgment it appears that the learned trial Court labouring under misconception of law that interest can only be awarded if the claimant is a banking company is absolutely erroneous and without any legal basis and on this point the learned trial Court failed to understand the law on this point as is prevalent in our country. Therefore, that observation of the learned trial Court has no legs to stand on and this part of the impugned judgment is liable to be struck off inasmuch as it is contrary to law as well as facts. 

 54. We have already noted that Appeal No. 94 of 2004 is filed under section 39(i)(vi) of the Act and in an appeal under that section the appellant can succeed only if he can bring the case the ambit of section 30 of the Act and we have already held in the earlier part of this judgment that they have failed to do so. Therefore, this appeal fails.

The other appeal, i.e. Appeal No. 66 of 2004, is filed under section 17 of the Act and in such an appeal the appellant can score a success only when the appellant can show that in making the award Rule of the Court, the Court has passed the decree in excess of the award or the decree is otherwise not in accordance with the award. None of these two elements are found present in Appeal No. 66 of 2004 and the appellant in this case also utterly failed to show that it comes within the ambit or mischief as contemplated in the said section. Thus, this appeal also fails. In view of our discussions in regard to the Appeal No. 10 of 2005 we are of the opinion that in the instant appeal the contractor has made out a case before the Umpire for awarding interest in their favour but the trial Court while making the award Rule of the Court denied the interest absolutely on an extraneous ground. Therefore, that observation of the trial Court is liable to be struck down.
